title: Optimal randomized memory-reallocation overhead
formal: Determine, up to absolute constant factors as \(\varepsilon\to0\), the optimal worst-case expected reallocation overhead \(F(\varepsilon)\) for online allocators with load at most \(1-\varepsilon\). The allocator stores objects in contiguous intervals of a fixed array and may relocate live objects after each insertion or deletion.
definitions: For every fixed real \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\) and integer array length \(M\ge1\), a request inserts a fresh object of positive integer size \(s\), or deletes a named live object. Valid finite sequences start empty and have total live size at most \((1-\varepsilon)M\) after every request. At each operation boundary, every live object occupies one contiguous interval of its size in \(\{0,\ldots,M-1\}\), and these intervals are disjoint. On an update involving an object \(x\), cost is \(1+\sum_y s(y)/s(x)\), where the sum is over objects live both before and after the update whose starting addresses change. This counts allocation changes at operation boundaries; local computation and allocation metadata are uncharged. The online rule may know \(M,\varepsilon\) but no future requests, and may use private randomness. A sequence is fixed independently of that randomness; allocations must always be valid. For a family of rules covering all \(M\), its overhead is the supremum, over all capacities, valid finite request sequences and individual update indices, of expected update cost. \(F(\varepsilon)\) is the infimum of those overheads over all such families. No history-independence or resizability constraint is imposed. The target measures each update’s expectation, rather than expected amortized cost or a high-probability bound.
why: A tight result would establish the intrinsic price of fragmentation when a general-purpose allocator operates close to full capacity.

context_blocks.text: The 2024 work studies low-overhead memory reallocation and its relationship with stronger resizability and history-independence guarantees. Those extra guarantees are not required for the target here.

Jin’s February 2026 paper gives an upper bound \(O((\log(1/\varepsilon))^4(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))^2)\) and a lower bound \(\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for general allocators. The new general lower bound improves the scope of earlier bounds restricted to resizable allocators.

progress.text: Polylogarithmic overhead is achieved, and a logarithmic lower bound is proved for general allocators.

answer_criterion: Supply an explicit function \(f(\varepsilon)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(c f(\varepsilon)\le F(\varepsilon)\le C f(\varepsilon)\) for absolute positive constants \(c,C\) and all sufficiently small positive \(\varepsilon\). Bounds only for resizable or history-independent allocators, or only for amortized expectation, do not establish the required matching result.

sentences: Objects of different sizes share one nearly full memory array.
Every object must occupy a contiguous interval.
An insertion or deletion may require moving other live objects.
Cost compares the total moved volume with the size of the updated object.
The remaining problem is the tight expected overhead as the unused fraction tends to zero.
